actions.reason: I didn't find a change likely to cut train_ir by 1.0%, so I'm stopping without spending evaluations on guesses. Both train functions are already heavily optimised in the current tip. BasicTokenizer.train counts pairs in C and updates a lazy heap, and RegexTokenizer.train keeps an occurrence index and sums per-merge deltas. By my rough estimate, without a profile, the Python work left inside the two train functions is a few percent of the ~324M-instruction run. Most of the rest is interpreter startup, the third-party regex import and pattern compile, and corpus generation in the harness, none of which minbpe can change. Earlier attempts that only did the same pair counting through C helpers, or de-duplicated visited chunks, measured ratios of 1.0001 to 1.0048. Cutting a further 1% would need about a third of the remaining train-loop work to go, and I found no algorithmic change of that size that keeps the outputs identical.

journal.text:
I read lineage_bench.py, minbpe/regex.py, minbpe/basic.py and minbpe/base.py, and ran two searches over imports and top-level definitions. I was looking for a change that would cut train_ir by 1.0%. I made no edits.

There are no measurements. I ran no sandbox evaluations and submitted no candidate. I stopped because I did not find a change I expected to reach the target, and I did not want to spend evaluations on guesses.

Both train functions in the current tip are already heavily optimised. BasicTokenizer.train counts pairs in C and updates a lazy heap. RegexTokenizer.train keeps an occurrence index and sums per-merge deltas. My view of how much Python work is left inside the merge loops is a rough estimate made without a profile. It is not a measurement.

Next time I will profile first. I will run lineage_bench.py under a profiler on both tokenizers, find where train_ir is actually spent, and only then pick a function to change.
